entities.summary:
Favorinus of Arelate (died c. 200 CE) was a highly distinctive and influential Roman sophist, orator, and Pyrrhonian skeptic philosopher who flourished during the reigns of Emperors Trajan and Hadrian, a pivotal figure in the intellectual efflorescence known as the Second Sophistic. Born in Arelate (modern Arles) in Gaul, Favorinus transcended his provincial origins to become a prominent intellectual in Rome and Athens, celebrated for his extraordinary rhetorical skill, formidable erudition, and provocative philosophical stance. His unique identity as a eunuch, coupled with his intellectual prowess, made him an object of both fascination and controversy in the Roman elite circles.

Favorinus's career was marked by a series of high-profile public performances and intellectual rivalries. He engaged in famed debates, including a well-documented confrontation with the Stoic Epictetus, and famously challenged the authority of Emperor Hadrian himself on a point of grammar, an act of intellectual courage that underscored his independent spirit. Though most of his extensive writings—which included philosophical treatises, historical works, and speeches—are now lost, fragments and accounts by contemporaries like Aulus Gellius and Philostratus reveal a master of Greek rhetoric, known for his elegant Atticizing style, sharp wit, and ability to argue persuasively on any side of an issue, embodying the skeptical tradition. His oratorical brilliance earned him the patronage of powerful figures, yet his sharp tongue and intellectual independence also led to periods of exile, notably from Rome under Hadrian.
